intro: Every other unit in this course handed you a story that someone else had already assembled from the evidence. This one hands you the evidence. It begins with two Chicago newspapers that reported the same 1894 strike and agreed on almost nothing, and it ends with a student who looked up at a street sign, asked why it said what it said, and found a lawsuit from 1884. In between it teaches the craft that turns a pile of documents, interviews, maps and numbers into a claim that other people can check and argue with.

The craft has rules, and the rules are the same whether the question is about the fall of Rome or the name of your school. Ask a question that evidence can answer. Find out who made each source, when, for whom and why, before you trust a word of it. Set sources against each other. Treat numbers and memories as sources that need the same tests. Get consent from the living and give credit to the dead. State the strongest case against your own claim, then answer it. Say plainly what you do not know. These rules are how historians disagree without simply shouting, and why their answers change when new evidence and new questions arrive.

By the end you will have done an inquiry of your own, from a local question through a source set, an argument, a presentation and an informed action, and you will be able to explain not only what you found but how your own thinking changed. That habit, asking for the evidence and stating the other side fairly, is the one thing in this course that you will use every day for the rest of your life.
bigQuestion: How do we know what we know about the past, and how can you build a claim about your own street, school, family or town that others can test and that leads to action?

timeline.t: Thucydides writes that he checked eyewitness accounts of the war against one another before trusting them
Lorenzo Valla uses the language of a document to prove the Donation of Constantine was a forgery
The first U.S. census counts about 3.9 million people; census counts become a basic source
The Fourteenth Amendment promises equal protection of the laws, a text courts will read in opposite ways
Ida B. Wells wins a lawsuit against a Tennessee railroad; the state supreme court reverses it in 1887
Wells publishes Southern Horrors, building her case against lynching from the white press's own reports
Chicago papers split over the Pullman strike; a federal commission takes sworn testimony
Congress creates the National Archives to keep the federal government's records
The Federal Writers' Project records interviews with thousands of formerly enslaved people
The Freedom of Information Act gives the public a legal right to request federal records
Signs for Ida B. Wells Drive replace Congress Parkway in downtown Chicago
The 1950 census answer sheets open to the public under the seventy-two-year rule

words.d: a source made at the time and by the people you are studying, such as a letter, a photograph, a court record or an interview with a witness
a later account, such as a history book or article, built by someone else from primary sources
asking who made a source, when, for whom and why before reading what it says
checking a claim against other independent sources before relying on it
the circumstances of the moment a source was made, which shape what its words meant
how far a source can be trusted for a particular question, which differs from question to question
a planned, recorded interview that preserves a person's memory as evidence
a debatable, specific statement that your evidence supports and a reasonable person could argue against
the strongest reasonable argument against your claim, stated fairly and then answered
a note telling a reader exactly where a piece of evidence came from so they can find and judge it
the history of how historians have interpreted a subject and why those interpretations changed
a specific request based on your evidence, addressed to the person or body with the power to act on it

test.q: Why did the chapter on historians' methods open with two newspapers reporting the same 1894 strike?
choices: To show that one paper was lying and the other was honest
To show that sources choose facts, people and words according to their makers and audiences
To prove that newspapers are never useful as sources
To show that the strike never happened
test.why: Neither paper simply lied; each selected and framed, which is why historians source before they trust.

test.q: A history book about the Pullman strike written in 1990 is what kind of source for a study of the strike?
choices: A primary source
An oral history
A secondary source
A statistic
test.why: It is a later account built from primary sources rather than a record from the time.

test.q: What is the first thing to write down about any new document, before reading its content?
choices: Its length and its best quotation
Whether you agree with it
How many websites mention it
Who made it, when, for whom and why
test.why: Sourcing comes first because those four facts change what the words can prove.

test.q: Two copies of the same wire report appear in five newspapers. Does that corroborate the report?
choices: No, because corroboration needs independent sources, not copies of one
Yes, because five is more than one
Yes, if the newspapers were in different cities
No, because newspapers can never corroborate anything
test.why: Corroboration requires independent agreement; reprints of one source count once.

test.q: According to the unit, what is the better question than 'Is this source biased?'
choices: Is this source old enough to be trusted?
What is this source reliable for, and for which questions?
Is this source a primary source?
Did the author have a college degree?
test.why: Every source has a perspective; the useful question is which purposes it can be trusted for.

test.q: The Black population of Chicago grew from about 44,000 in 1910 to about 109,000 in 1920. What can that census figure alone NOT tell you?
choices: That the population grew
Roughly how many people were counted in each year
Why people came and what they found when they arrived
Which decade is being compared
test.why: A statistic shows a pattern; causes and experiences need other sources such as letters, interviews and newspapers.

test.q: Which of these is a requirement of research ethics as the unit describes it?
choices: Recording interviews secretly to get honest answers
Using only sources more than a century old
Copying a historian's wording without credit if the facts are true
Getting informed consent before recording and giving credit for every borrowed idea
test.why: Respect for persons and honesty about credit are the two duties the unit stresses.

test.q: In a claim-evidence-reasoning argument, what is the reasoning?
choices: Your own explanation of why the evidence supports the claim
The list of sources at the end
A quotation that repeats the claim
The date of the event being argued about
test.why: Evidence does not speak for itself; reasoning connects it to the claim in the writer's words.

test.q: Why do interpretations of an event such as Reconstruction change over time?
choices: Because the facts of the past change
Because new evidence, new questions and new people with different experiences enter the conversation
Because each generation of historians is less careful than the last
Because textbooks are rewritten by law every decade
test.why: Historiography changes as archives open, as questions shift and as historians from once-excluded groups join the field.

test.q: Which local question passes the feasibility check most easily?
choices: What every resident of the ward believed in 1919
What a great-grandmother who left no papers privately felt about the riot
How every migration to Chicago in the twentieth century happened
When and why the local school received its name, using board records and newspapers
test.why: The school question has records that exist, can be reached, can be read and can be finished in a semester.

test.q: Why did the student in the capstone story treat the gap between Wells's life and Chicago's honors as her real question?
choices: Because the gap showed the records were false
Because Wells had never lived in Chicago
Because when a city gives an honor reveals what it valued and whose voices it heard at that moment
Because the gap could be closed by a single source
test.why: The timing of the 1940s housing project, the 2017 stalled proposal and the 2018 renaming tells a story about power and cost.

test.q: A student comparing a block on Sanborn maps from 1894, 1925 and 1950 can learn which of these?
choices: How the buildings changed in shape, material and use
The names and ages of every resident
The price of each house
What residents thought of their landlords
test.why: Sanborn maps record buildings, not people; residents come from the census, prices from deeds, opinions from interviews.

test.q: What should an interviewer do BEFORE the recorder starts?
choices: Write the transcript
Explain the project and how the recording will be used, and get the person's consent
Check the person's memory against the census
Ask the leading questions first
test.why: Consent must be informed and given in advance, and the person must know they can stop or withdraw.

test.q: Which sequence best describes how to answer a counterclaim?
choices: Ignore it, then restate your claim more loudly
State a weak version of it and dismiss it
Agree with it and drop your claim
State it fairly, concede what is true in it, then rebut the rest with specific evidence
test.why: Steelmanning the other side and conceding its true parts makes the rebuttal more believable.

test.q: Which of these is informed action as the unit defines it?
choices: A letter to a U.S. senator demanding that Chicago rename a street
A social media post saying history matters
A one-page proposal to the local school council with the claim, two pieces of evidence and a source list attached
A summary of the project stored in a folder
test.why: Informed action carries evidence to a body with jurisdiction; a senator cannot rename a Chicago street.

write.prompt: Make a claim about a local question of your own choosing, such as a street or school name, a family's move or a law's effect. Support it with at least three sources you have found, explain your reasoning, state the strongest counterclaim fairly and answer it, and end by saying what your evidence cannot show.
tips: State your claim in one sentence that a reasonable person could argue against; a fact is not a claim.
For each source, note who made it, when, for whom and why, and use at least one primary source and one person's interview or memoir.
Explain in your own words why each piece of evidence supports the claim; do not let a quotation stand alone.
Write the counterclaim as its own supporters would write it, concede what is true, then rebut with specific evidence.
Name the limits of your evidence honestly: what record you could not find, whom you could not interview, and what you would do next.
